01 / THE POWER OF STARTING

Same habit.
Very different futures.

Compounding means your returns can earn returns, too. For investments, that growth isn’t a fixed interest payment—it rises and falls with the market. Time gives it room to build.

01

Your deposits start it.

The part you control is the habit: a contribution each payday, even if it starts small.

02 / GIVE YOUR MONEY A HOME

Two accounts.
One future you.

A retirement account is a container with tax benefits. The investments inside it do the growing. You can use a 401(k) and a Roth IRA together—you don’t have to pick just one.

THROUGH YOUR EMPLOYER

The 401(k)

You choose how much of each paycheck to invest. Your employer’s plan provides a menu of investments and may add a matching contribution.

$24,5002026 employee limit
Under age 50 · across pre-tax + Roth

WHY IT HELPS

  • Payroll deductions make saving automatic.
  • A match adds money you don’t have to contribute yourself.
  • Pre-tax contributions generally reduce current federal taxable income. Growth isn’t taxed each year.
  • A higher contribution ceiling than an IRA.

WHAT TO KNOW

  • Investment choices and plan fees vary.
  • Pre-tax withdrawals are generally taxable income.
  • Early withdrawals can trigger taxes and a 10% additional tax; exceptions apply.
  • Employer money may need time to become fully yours (“vesting”). Your own contributions are always yours.
What does “50% match up to 6%” mean?

At a $60,000 salary, investing 6% is $3,600 a year. A 50% match on that amount adds $1,800 from your employer. That’s $5,400 invested, before market changes. Contributing more than 6% won’t earn more under this example formula. Check your plan’s rules, vesting, and per-paycheck matching policy.

What about a Roth 401(k)?

If offered, it takes after-tax contributions and allows qualified tax-free withdrawals. It shares the employee limit with your pre-tax 401(k), but does not have the Roth IRA’s income ceiling. Its withdrawal rules differ from a Roth IRA. Employer contributions can have a different tax treatment; check your plan.

Plan basics & vesting: U.S. Department of Labor ↗

OPENED BY YOU

The Roth IRA

You contribute money you’ve already paid income tax on. Invest it, let it grow, and qualified retirement withdrawals—including the growth—are tax-free.

$7,5002026 combined IRA limit
Under age 50 · Roth + traditional IRAs

WHY IT HELPS

  • Decades of potential growth can come out tax-free when qualified.
  • You choose the provider and investments.
  • No required minimum withdrawals during the original owner’s lifetime.
  • Regular contributions can generally be withdrawn tax- and penalty-free.

WHAT TO KNOW

  • No tax deduction for contributions today.
  • Income and earned compensation affect eligibility.
  • The annual limit is relatively small.
  • Early access to earnings is different from access to contributions; taxes and penalties may apply.
When are withdrawals tax-free?

For a typical retirement withdrawal, you must be at least 59½ and satisfy the five-tax-year rule, starting with the first tax year you contributed to a Roth IRA. Other qualifying exceptions exist. Regular contributions come out first under IRS ordering rules; conversions have separate rules. Withdrawing contributions also removes their future growth potential.

IRS withdrawal rules ↗

Why might this be useful in your 30s?

A long horizon gives investment growth more time to accumulate. Paying tax now can make sense if your tax rate is lower today than when you withdraw. But being young doesn’t automatically make Roth better: current taxes, future income, and your budget still matter.

Roth IRA overview: IRS ↗

The 2026 limits are ceilings, not starting requirements. You can start with an amount your budget supports. IRA contributions also cannot exceed eligible taxable compensation (spousal IRA rules may help married couples). Employer contributions don’t use your $24,500 employee allowance; a separate 2026 combined 401(k) cap is generally the lesser of $72,000 or 100% of compensation, excluding catch-ups.

Limits reviewed September 26, 2026. They can change annually. These examples use under-50 limits; age-50+ catch-ups and special age-60–63 rules are not modeled. Verify the current IRS limits ↗

2026 Roth IRA eligibility: check your income

For direct Roth IRA contributions, the allowed amount phases out as modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) rises: $153,000–$168,000 for single/head-of-household filers and $242,000–$252,000 for married filing jointly. Below the lower threshold, the full limit may be available; at or above the upper one, direct contributions are not allowed.

Married filing separately and living with a spouse at any point in the year generally has a $0–$10,000 range. If you lived apart all year, different rules apply. MAGI isn’t always the same as salary. The calculators don’t determine your eligibility; confirm before contributing. IRS contribution and eligibility rules ↗

Roth or traditional? It’s about when you pay tax.

A simple IRA comparison. A workplace 401(k) may also offer both tax treatments.
The questionRoth IRATraditional IRA
Tax break today?No. Contributions use after-tax money.Possibly. A deduction depends on income and workplace plan coverage.
Taxes as investments grow?No annual tax on gains inside the account.No annual tax on gains inside the account.
Taxes in retirement?Qualified withdrawals are tax-free.Deductible contributions and earnings are generally taxed as ordinary income.
Often worth considering when…Your tax rate now is relatively low, or you value tax-free income later.A deduction is available and your tax rate now is higher than you expect later.
Main tradeoff?You give up a possible deduction now.You face future taxes and required minimum withdrawals.

Make the comparison fair.

With $100 of pre-tax earnings and a 22% tax rate, you could invest $100 in a deductible traditional account or $78 in a Roth. If both grow 10× and the withdrawal tax rate is still 22%, each leaves $780 to spend. Roth is not “extra growth”—its advantage depends on tax rates and circumstances.

You can keep both doors open.

A pre-tax workplace 401(k) plus a Roth IRA can give you a mix of taxable and tax-free retirement income. If you choose a traditional IRA, verify the deduction rather than assuming it. Nondeductible contributions require tracking to avoid taxing the same money twice.

IRS: contributions and deductions ↗

03 / PUT THE MONEY TO WORK

The account holds it.
The investments grow it.

Adding money to an IRA can leave it sitting in cash. Choose an investment, complete the purchase, and confirm that future deposits are invested, too.

An ETF is a basket you can buy.

An exchange-traded fund holds a collection of investments. Shares trade throughout the day, like a stock. Broad index ETFs can provide access to many companies without choosing each one yourself.

A mutual fund is a basket, too.

It typically trades once a day at its calculated share value. Some have minimum purchases. Many work well with automatic deposits, and they are common in 401(k) menus.

“Index” is the strategy; ETF or mutual fund is the format. An index fund follows a defined market benchmark. Both formats can be low-cost and diversified—or concentrated and expensive. Read what the fund actually owns.

01 / WHAT’S INSIDE?

Check the holdings.

Look for a clear role: U.S. stocks, international stocks, or bonds. Two funds may own many of the same companies.

02 / WHAT DOES IT COST?

Read the expense ratio.

0.05% costs about $5 per year per $10,000 held; 1% costs about $100. Also check account fees, trading costs, and sales charges.

03 / CAN YOU STICK WITH IT?

Understand the risk.

Stock funds can fall sharply. Diversification spreads risk but cannot prevent losses. Money needed soon belongs in a different plan.

04 / MAKE IT REPEATABLE.

Automate and review.

Check automatic dollar purchases, fractional shares, and minimums at your provider. Reinvest dividends and review your mix annually.

LEARNING FROM PROFESSOR G

A simple, three-part stock portfolio.

Watch Investing Simplified ↗

Professor G describes an approach built around a foundational stock fund, a growth fund, and a dividend/value fund. Here is what those roles mean. The funds below are research examples, not a personalized shopping list.

01 · The foundation

A broad U.S. stock fund spreads your investment across many businesses. VOO tracks the S&P 500; VTI covers a broader U.S. market. They overlap heavily, so owning both is not automatically more diversified.

02 · A growth tilt

A fund such as SCHG focuses on large U.S. growth companies. It can increase concentration in companies already in the foundation. “Growth” describes a style, not a promise of higher returns.

03 · Dividend / value

A dividend-focused fund such as SCHD emphasizes dividend-paying U.S. companies. Dividends can be reinvested, but aren’t free extra returns or guaranteed payments. Consider total return: price changes plus distributions.

Keep the tradeoffs in view. This is a stock-focused approach, not the traditional U.S. stocks + international stocks + bonds “three-fund portfolio.” It can overlap, remains exposed to market declines, and does not by itself provide broad international or bond diversification. No allocation is prescribed here, and past performance does not establish future outperformance. A 401(k) may offer different funds with similar roles.

Prefer one decision? Consider a low-cost target-date index fund.

Choose a date near your expected retirement, then compare fees and the investment mix. These funds typically combine stocks and bonds and become more conservative over time. They can be an all-in-one approach, but funds with the same year can have different risks—and none guarantees enough retirement income. SEC guide to target-date funds ↗

How this calculator works & what it leaves out

All projections start at $0. We convert the effective annual return to a monthly rate: (1 + annual return)1/12 − 1. Monthly deposits are added after each month’s growth. Returns are constant for illustration, with dividends reinvested. Use a return net of investment and account fees. Actual returns vary; losses and their timing matter.

Monthly contributions are capped using 2026 under-50 limits: $7,500/year for IRAs and $24,500/year for employee 401(k) deferrals. The 401(k) calculation also caps employee contributions at entered salary and combined employee/employer contributions at the lesser of $72,000 or salary. Salary and limits stay unchanged for the entire illustration. The Roth calculator assumes sufficient taxable compensation, full income eligibility, and no other IRA contributions. It cannot check your actual eligibility.

The optional buying-power view discounts the final balance and chart by 2.5% annual inflation. Contribution and growth totals remain nominal dollars and reconcile to the nominal balance shown below the result. No withdrawal taxes, penalties, changes in tax law, contribution increases, catch-ups, or retirement withdrawals are modeled. A Roth result is tax-free only if withdrawal requirements are met. The 401(k) result is before any withdrawal taxes, whether your plan uses pre-tax, Roth, or both.

05 / TURN UNDERSTANDING INTO ACTION

Your first move
can be small.

You don’t need to max out an account this week. Pick one useful step, take it, then make the next contribution easier.

01 / GET YOUR FOOTING

Protect the habit.

Keep bills current, make required debt payments, and build an accessible cash buffer. Look at expensive debt alongside investing: paying it down saves interest without market risk. Avoid investing money you’ll need soon.

02 / CHECK YOUR BENEFITS

Understand your match.

Ask HR about the 401(k), match formula, vesting, and fees. If your budget allows, contributing enough for the full match is often a strong first retirement step. Confirm the investments selected for your deposits.

03 / BUILD YOUR ROUTINE

Choose. Invest. Repeat.

Compare IRA providers and eligibility, then choose a simple investment approach. Automate an affordable amount. Consider increasing it when you get a raise, and review your contributions and fund mix once a year.
